https://www.baltictimes.com/lithuania_ex.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Lithuania expects Latvia to seek equipment, personnel for border security 2026-07-23 LETA/BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Lithuanian Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas expects Latvia to request technical equipment, including thermal imagers, in addition to personnel to strengthen its border security. "We are in talks with the Latvian side. I hope they will express a need not only for physical capabilities and border guards on the ground (...) they also lack thermal imagers and night vision devices. Perhaps not as a gift, but we could lend them to strengthen their capabilities. There are many options, and I believe this is a conversation between our border leadership and theirs regarding specific needs," Katelynas told reporters on Thursday. The minister said specific assistance should be negotiated by border services rather than politicians to ensure solutions are tailored to Latvia's actual requirements. During the first six months of this year, secondary migration from Latvia to Lithuania surged from just over 300 to more than 1,200 foreigners. While Lithuania is already sending teams of border guards to assist Latvia, it does not intend to provide the full 100 officers requested. Since early July, nine officers from the Lithuanian State Border Guard Service, accompanied by service dogs, have been deployed to Latvia to help secure the border with Belarus. A second group of border guards followed on July 15. Saulius Nekrasevicius, deputy commander of the Lithuanian State Border Guard Service, said Latvia is currently the country most affected by instrumentalized migration. He reported approximately 150 attempted illegal border crossings in a single day, a figure comparable to the most difficult periods Lithuania experienced in 2021-2022. Nekrasevicius added that Lithuania cannot reduce its own security presence on the Belarusian border, meaning the scale of aid and the number of specialists sent to Latvia are being constantly coordinated with Latvia. The interior ministers of Lithuania and Latvia have also signed a cooperation agreement to combat crime, aimed at dismantling organized migrant smuggling networks. The rise in secondary migration has also caused problems for Poland. In July 2025, Poland reinstated checks at its borders with Lithuania and Germany, with controls currently in place until October 1. Katelynas said he discussed the situation in Latvia with his Polish counterparts, and border plenipotentiaries from Lithuania and Poland were scheduled to meet on Thursday to discuss improving inspection procedures. According to Katelynas, Latvia should negotiate directly with Polish border services for additional assistance. According to Lithjuanian State Border Guard Service data, more than 8,000 migrants have attempted to enter Latvia from Belarus this year, either being detained and returned or deterred on the Belarusian side. This figure is nearly nine times higher than the number of attempted entries into Lithuania from Belarus. Comments Related Articles Subscribe Log In Ads Please enter your username and password. Dean Best August 17, 2026 2 min read Lithuania-based seafood processors Nordian Group and Norvelita are to move into private-equity ownership. INVL Asset Management, based in Vilnius, Lithuania's capital, has signed agreements to buy the businesses. Combined, the seafood companies generate revenue of €200m ($231.8m), their prospective new owner said. Nordian Group is a fish processor and wholesaler that supplies Lithuanian retail chains. Last year, the company, which employs more than 170 staff, booked revenue of €46.3m. Norvelita is the larger of the two businesses. It specialises in salmon and exports around 85% of its production to western Europe. In 2025, the company brought in revenues of €152.7m. It has 650 staff. Nerijus Drobavičius, a partner for INVL's Private Equity Fund II, said the firm wants to create "a strong, internationally competitive fish processing group". Drobavičius added: "Norvelita's experience and stable export business will complement Nordian Group's growth ambitions. We see clear synergies between the two companies – from joint raw material procurement to the development and expansion of new, higher value-added product categories in the EU. This is an investment in a sector where demand for quality products keeps growing, and it puts us in a position to give the end consumer a clearly better choice." The founders of both companies will remain minority shareholders and "will continue to help build value in the group", a statement read. Ramūnas Gaižauskas, Nordian Group's founder and main shareholder, said: "We have built one of the strongest fresh fish supply businesses in the Baltic States. Now, we are entering the next stage of growth. Together with our partners, we will be able to implement our ambitious expansion plans much more rapidly, strengthen our position in export markets, expand into new fish and seafood segments, and create even greater value for our customers, employees, and shareholders." Jordanas Kenstavičius, Norvelita's founder and principal shareholder, said the deal would "provide the opportunity to further invest in production capacity and people, while ensuring that the company continues to grow by maintaining quality and customer trust". "Seafood groups Nordian Group, Norvelita sold to PE firm" was originally created and published by Just Food , a GlobalData owned brand. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany Bundesregierung/Tobias Koch/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany Bundesregierung/Tobias Koch/Shutterstock Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Germany’s Merz pledges €1bn in military aid to Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks German chancellor also announces €350m for repairs to energy sector as Moscow targets Ukrainian infrastructure before winter. What we know on day 1,685 Guardian staff and agencies Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Germany won’t be intimidated into dropping its support for Ukraine, chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Sunday as he announced €1bn ($1.1bn) in military aid during a visit to Kyiv. Merz said Germany would fund the joint production of drones designed to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, adding that “significant technical breakthroughs” in recent weeks were speeding up production. Speaking alongside Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Merz also announced €350m for repairs to the energy sector. German officials said company executives who travelled with Merz had signed 14 agreements with Ukraine worth about €6.6bn . They included an agreement with Germany’s Diehl Defence for the supply of IRIS-T air defence missiles, as well as a deal for radar equipment with Hensoldt and for jet drone interceptors with Quantum Systems. Air raid sirens and explosions rang out ⁠repeatedly across the Ukrainian capital during the German chancellor’s visit . A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by tens of thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Later on Sunday, a Russian ⁠airstrike ​hit Kharkiv, Ukraine’s ⁠second-biggest ⁠city, ​killing ‌one ‌person ‌and injured another six , mayor ‌Ihor Terekhov ​said ⁠on Telegram. View image in fullscreen A vehicle burns after Russia’s latest attack on Kharkiv. Photograph: Andrii Marienko/AP In Kyiv, Merz said Germany’s financial help was not only about protecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity . “We do it deeply in our own interest, for it is a matter of Europe’s security,” he said, ​adding that Russia was carrying out cyber-attacks and disinformation campaigns targeting European democracy. Russia has said accusations of hybrid warfare are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria. Zelenskyy said on Sunday he believed Russia might have ⁠shared jet-drone technology with its ally North Korea . Earlier in the war, ⁠North Korea supplied Russia with millions of artillery shells, and it has since provided ballistic missiles that Moscow regularly uses ⁠to attack Ukrainian cities. Asked if Russia had shared with North Korea ​the technology behind its latest generation ‌of jet-powered drones, ‌Zelenskyy told journalists: “They [Russia] are sharing with North Korea all the technologies. ‌I don’t know about the ballistic and etc but I think yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles.” Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military has again used drones to ⁠deliver food and medicine to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky ⁠in southern ⁠Ukraine , ​ foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday. Oleshky, a frontline town ⁠on the Dnipro River, which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has become “a hell on earth” under Russian occupation since 2022, according to residents. Sybiha, who has previously accused Russia of starving residents, said the latest delivery contained almost four metric tons of food and medicine. Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said last month that Russia had not ​agreed ​to Ukrainian proposals to ​allow civilians to evacuate. As Zelenskyy on Sunday said the US wanted to hold a new round of peace talks with Ukraine and Russia by the end of October, India said it was seeking a greater role in brokering an end to the war , the foreign minister said. Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said at a Munich Security Conference in New Delhi on Sunday that India had been advocating for a peace deal “for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy, so we have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard”. He said India was starting with Black Sea safety of shipping but also including discussions about grain and energy exports and “on non-attack possibilities”. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/ryanair-s.text: Helena Vesty Updated Wed, October 28, 2026 at 5:23 AM UTC 0 Warsaw has two Christmas markets (Image: Getty) Ryanair has launched a new route for cheap breaks this winter , just in time to take advantage of the Christmas markets. The budget airline announced that the first flight has taken off in its new winter 2026 route from Manchester to Warsaw Modlin in Poland. Ryanair bosses revealed the news yesterday (October 27), saying it it will operate six weekly flights on this "exciting new winter 2026 route, providing UK customers with even more choice at Europe's lowest fares". The new route gives Brits the chance to enjoy Warsaw's two Christmas markets, including the huge Jarmark Warszawski at Plac Defilad, by the Palace of Culture and Science, and the traditional, historic market in the Old Town along the city walls. Both markets run from November to January and boast free entry, featuring classic winter scenes of chalets, Christmas trees, and an open-air ice rink. Ryanair's full winter 2026 schedule is available to book now via the Ryanair app and website in time for cheap winter and Christmas breaks. Ryanair is launching a host of new routes for winter 2026 (Image: Getty) The first flight comes after Ryanair unveiled its newly expanded winter schedule last month, with 22 new routes from UK airports with Birmingham, Edinburgh, Liverpool, and London airports benefiting the most. Ryanair also announced that it was adding nineteenth-based aircraft at Manchester Airport this winter, helping it to run one extra route from the North West hub. Ryanair is increasing its flight frequencies on another 26 routes from Manchester, including holiday hotspots like Malaga, Palma de Mallorca and Madrid, as well as city break destinations like Barcelona, Belfast, Venice, Porto, Prague and Krakow. Eye-catching flights among the list included the new winter sunshine route from Birmingham to Marrakech, which regularly enjoys mild winter temperatures. The bulk of the other routes are to northern and western European destinations where more festive pleasures are on the itinerary.
